cases.context: Customer-facing Django service deployed to the public internet; production settings are confirmed in the request.
cases.precondition: DEBUG=True is active for publicly reachable production responses.
cases.prompt: Review a Django PR: the production settings module sets DEBUG=True, and error responses are publicly accessible. State the specific risk.
cases.chosen: Flag the active production debug setting: error pages may expose project settings, code excerpts or local data. Disable it for this deployment.
cases.rejected: The setting is a harmless optimization: debug pages only improve developer diagnostics and do not affect production confidentiality in this service.
cases.review_note: Deployment context is decisive; do not infer a leaked key from DEBUG alone.

cases.context: Django runs only on an isolated local development laptop; production imports a separate settings file with DEBUG=False.
cases.precondition: No reachable production process uses this development configuration.
cases.prompt: A pull request shows DEBUG=True in settings/dev.py. Production settings separately set DEBUG=False and the dev server is not reachable. Review severity.
cases.chosen: Do not report confirmed production debug leakage from the dev-only file. Verify that production actually imports the intended hardened settings module.
cases.rejected: Report critical production information disclosure solely from the presence of DEBUG=True in the dev-only file, despite the distinct production configuration.
cases.review_note: A standalone grep match is insufficient without deployment conditions.

cases.context: A production Django signing key value is committed verbatim to a public repository; the actual value is intentionally withheld here.
cases.precondition: The reviewer has independent evidence a real production key was pushed; only redacted metadata is provided in this task.
cases.prompt: Security review of deployment settings: investigators confirm the live SECRET_KEY was committed in public git history. The actual secret is redacted.
cases.chosen: Treat the verified live signing key disclosure as a security finding. Rotate the affected key, protect dependent sessions, and remove public exposure.
cases.rejected: The key was only present in settings, so retaining it in public history is safe; changing it would add unnecessary operational disruption.
cases.review_note: Do not include a real credential in the casebook, even if it was previously exposed.

cases.context: README documentation uses the literal text EXAMPLE_FAKE_KEY_NOT_VALID and clarifies that it is not installed anywhere.
cases.precondition: There is no evidence that the placeholder is a live secret or that the application loads it.
cases.prompt: Review a README snippet: SECRET_KEY="EXAMPLE_FAKE_KEY_NOT_VALID" appears in a commented example; production reads a secure environment variable.
cases.chosen: The documented placeholder is not evidence of a live key leak. Verify the running configuration and scan for real credentials separately.
cases.rejected: This confirms a production signing-key compromise; revoke all sessions immediately because every string named SECRET_KEY must be a real secret.
cases.review_note: Detecting the variable name is not equivalent to finding an exposed credential.

cases.context: A public webhook probe takes arbitrary caller URLs; the backend follows redirects, and the network has routes to internal services.
cases.precondition: Untrusted input is sent through an unrestricted request client which may access internal destinations.
cases.prompt: Assess this webhook checker: accepts a customer-provided URL, follows 30x redirects automatically, and can access internal network destinations.
cases.chosen: Flag an SSRF path: untrusted destinations and redirects can reach internal endpoints. Constrain resolved targets at connect time and restrict redirects.
cases.rejected: There is no request-boundary risk because the first URL must use HTTPS; redirects and internal reachability do not change the security outcome.
cases.review_note: SSRF requires evaluating trust boundaries and network reachability, not only HTTP scheme.

cases.context: The application selects a fixed partner host from a server-owned mapping and blocks redirects; other egress controls were not independently audited.
cases.precondition: User input is only an approved partner identifier, not an arbitrary URL or destination.
cases.prompt: Review a server-side partner callback using a fixed mapping of partner IDs to trusted destinations, no redirects, and outbound filtering.
cases.chosen: The described controls reduce the obvious arbitrary-destination SSRF route. Check resolution and network enforcement before claiming complete protection.
cases.rejected: All SSRF is impossible whenever a service keeps a partner allowlist. There is no reason to test destination resolution or egress bypass.
cases.review_note: Do not claim absolute safety from incomplete evidence of defense in depth.

cases.context: A public fork pull-request workflow checks untrusted changes; its automation token is configured with permissions: write-all.
cases.precondition: Untrusted code may execute inside an automation job holding broad repository permissions.
cases.prompt: Review a GitHub Actions workflow that runs untrusted pull-request build scripts and grants GITHUB_TOKEN permissions: write-all for the job.
cases.chosen: Flag unnecessarily broad token authority for an untrusted build. Reduce to contents: read and avoid granting write scopes to the PR job.
cases.rejected: Granting write-all is a best practice because build scripts need full access to the repository by default, including write access to source.
cases.review_note: The risk is privilege exposure, not proof that a credential has already been stolen.

cases.context: A dependency test job only reads code, explicitly sets contents: read, and never accesses secrets or write scopes.
cases.precondition: The only supported workflow operations are checkout and unprivileged test execution.
cases.prompt: A GitHub Actions workflow runs lint and tests on PRs, sets permissions: { contents: read }, and does not pass secrets to the job.
cases.chosen: The supplied token scope is consistent with least privilege for this test job. Do not report a confirmed write-token exposure without more evidence.
cases.rejected: This PR job has a critical repository-write escalation because every GITHUB_TOKEN can modify source, even with permissions restricted to contents: read.
cases.review_note: Avoid treating mere token presence as evidence of excessive permissions.

cases.context: A release workflow prints the entire secret value after base64 encoding it; actual secret bytes are omitted from the review request.
cases.precondition: Encoding changes secret representation and GitHub log redaction may not catch transformed values.
cases.prompt: Inspect a release job that base64-encodes a production token and writes the resulting value to build logs; the sensitive value is redacted in this prompt.
cases.chosen: Flag potential secret disclosure via transformed log output. Stop printing the encoded value, rotate if exposed, and audit access to the logs.
cases.rejected: The output is safe because GitHub automatically masks every possible encoded form of secrets; base64 logging cannot expose a credential.
cases.review_note: Security guidance warns that automatic secret masking is not guaranteed for transformations.

cases.context: A release job receives a deploy token through a protected secret environment variable, and the supplied steps never print it.
cases.precondition: Runtime access and external action trust still require review, but no disclosure path is shown.
cases.prompt: Review a protected GitHub Actions release job that injects DEPLOY_TOKEN from secrets and uses it only for an authenticated deploy operation.
cases.chosen: Secret injection alone is not evidence of exfiltration. Review third-party actions and access controls, but avoid inventing an observed token leak.
cases.rejected: Any GitHub Actions job using a secret is already compromised, regardless of the job permissions or whether a disclosure path exists.
cases.review_note: The finding must follow evidence of actual exposure or untrusted execution.

cases.context: A Node production service makes an outbound HTTPS request to its payment service, with TLS validation explicitly disabled.
cases.precondition: rejectUnauthorized:false applies on the production https client for sensitive requests.
cases.prompt: Assess a payment client that creates https.Agent({ rejectUnauthorized: false }) and uses it for production requests carrying checkout metadata.
cases.chosen: Flag disabled peer-certificate rejection on production HTTPS connections. Restore certificate and hostname checks and investigate whether traffic was exposed.
cases.rejected: No TLS authenticity risk exists because encryption still occurs; ignoring certificate validation is harmless when the HTTP URL begins with https.
cases.review_note: TLS encryption without certificate authentication does not prove server identity.

cases.context: The TLS bypass exists only inside a unit test using a local disposable mock server; production uses the standard verified HTTPS agent.
cases.precondition: No test-only override is imported or activated by production code paths.
cases.prompt: Review a Node test fixture with rejectUnauthorized:false against a locally controlled self-signed mock; live services use the default HTTPS agent.
cases.chosen: Do not report confirmed production certificate bypass solely from the isolated test fixture. Confirm it cannot be enabled in deployment builds.
cases.rejected: The presence of rejectUnauthorized:false in any test proves the customer-facing payment client disables certificate verification in production.
cases.review_note: Severity depends on execution context and reachability, not just the token literal.

notice: Illustrative hypothetical application situations grounded in public guidance. DRAFT ONLY: source URLs are not pinned, content has not received independent human security review, and no network acceptance is claimed.
